beats.text: Both hosts at their microphones; the woman speaks to the man
spoken: Welcome back to the show. Today: why cities are planting tiny forests.
Tiny forests? Like... bonsai trees?
Not quite. Picture an empty lot the size of a tennis court, packed with native trees.

beats.text: The man leans in and asks
spoken: Packed how tightly?

beats.text: The woman explains, counting on her fingers
spoken: Three to five saplings per square metre, in enriched soil. It is the method of Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki.
So the trees compete for light and grow fast.
Exactly. Supporters say a tiny forest can sustain itself in about three years.
And what do cities get out of it?
Cooler streets, more insects and birds, and a place for schoolchildren to learn.
Sounds great. But I am guessing there is a catch.
Critics say the evidence is still thin. Many projects are too young to measure, and dense planting can mean many saplings die.
And urban ecologists agree: a tiny forest is no substitute for protecting existing large trees, which store far more carbon.

beats.text: The woman smiles and signs off
spoken: Plant small, protect big. Thanks for listening!

story.title: Tiny Forests podcast
story.setting: A cozy podcast studio with warm soft light, wooden desk, two studio microphones on arms, foam panels and a few potted plants behind; realistic, steady medium shot.

subjects.words: a woman podcast host in her early 30s with shoulder-length dark hair, wearing a green sweater, seated at the left microphone
a man podcast host in his early 30s with short brown hair and a beard, wearing a grey t-shirt, seated at the right microphone

beats.text: Both hosts at their microphones; the woman speaks to the man
spoken: Welcome back to the show. Today: why cities are planting tiny forests.
Tiny forests? Like... bonsai trees?
Not quite. Picture an empty lot the size of a tennis court, packed with native trees.

beats.text: The man leans in and asks
spoken: Packed how tightly?

beats.text: The woman explains, counting on her fingers
spoken: Three to five saplings per square metre, in enriched soil. It is the method of Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki.
So the trees compete for light and grow fast.
Exactly. Supporters say a tiny forest can sustain itself in about three years.
And what do cities get out of it?
Cooler streets, more insects and birds, and a place for schoolchildren to learn.
Sounds great. But I am guessing there is a catch.
Critics say the evidence is still thin. Many projects are too young to measure, and dense planting can mean many saplings die.
And urban ecologists agree: a tiny forest is no substitute for protecting existing large trees, which store far more carbon.

beats.text: The woman smiles and signs off
spoken: Plant small, protect big. Thanks for listening!
